claim: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) infects the majority of the human population worldwide.
source: Human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a prevalent pathogen of the beta-herpesvirus family, infecting the majority of the human population worldwide (Staras et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Staras et al., 2006

claim: Following primary infection, HCMV persists through the lifetime of the host by establishing latency.
source: Following primary infection, HCMV persists through the lifetime of the host by establishing latency.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about HCMV infection

claim: In the latent state, no viral progeny is produced but the virus maintains the capacity to reactivate.
source: In the latent state, no viral progeny is produced but the virus maintains the capacity to reactivate.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about viral latency

claim: Reactivation in immunocompromised individuals, such as transplant recipients and HIV patients, leads to severe illness and mortality.
source: Reactivation in immunocompromised individuals, such as transplant recipients and HIV patients, leads to severe illness and mortality (Crough and Khanna, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crough and Khanna, 2009

claim: There is no treatment that targets the latent stage of HCMV.
source: Despite the significant health burden that accompanies HCMV reactivation from latency, to date there is no treatment that targets the latent stage and the processes governing latency and reactivation are far from fully understood.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about current HCMV treatments

claim: HCMV has a wide cell tropism within its human host.
source: HCMV has a wide cell tropism within its human host (Mocarski and Shenk, 2013), with most cell types supporting lytic replication (Sinzger et al., 2008a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mocarski and Shenk, 2013 and Sinzger et al., 2008a

claim: Most cell types support lytic replication of HCMV.
source: HCMV has a wide cell tropism within its human host (Mocarski and Shenk, 2013), with most cell types supporting lytic replication (Sinzger et al., 2008a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sinzger et al., 2008a

claim: Latent HCMV infection has been characterized in CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) in vivo.
source: In contrast, latent infection has so far been characterized in cells of the early myeloid lineage, including CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) and CD14+ monocytes in vivo (Mendelson et al., 1996; Taylor-Wiedeman et al., 1991; von Laer et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mendelson et al., 1996; Taylor-Wiedeman et al., 1991; von Laer et al., 1995

claim: Latent HCMV infection has been characterized in CD14+ monocytes in vivo.
source: In contrast, latent infection has so far been characterized in cells of the early myeloid lineage, including CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) and CD14+ monocytes in vivo (Mendelson et al., 1996; Taylor-Wiedeman et al., 1991; von Laer et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mendelson et al., 1996; Taylor-Wiedeman et al., 1991; von Laer et al., 1995

claim: CD14+ monocytes are short-lived cells.
source: Since CD14+ monocytes are short-lived cells it has been proposed that the latent reservoir resides in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) (Slobedman et al., 2010) and that latent monocytes support viral spread and persistence within the infected host (Stevenson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about monocyte lifespan

claim: The latent HCMV reservoir resides in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs).
source: Since CD14+ monocytes are short-lived cells it has been proposed that the latent reservoir resides in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) (Slobedman et al., 2010) and that latent monocytes support viral spread and persistence within the infected host (Stevenson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Slobedman et al., 2010

claim: Latent monocytes support viral spread and persistence within the infected host.
source: Since CD14+ monocytes are short-lived cells it has been proposed that the latent reservoir resides in hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) (Slobedman et al., 2010) and that latent monocytes support viral spread and persistence within the infected host (Stevenson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stevenson et al., 2014

claim: Latent cells in HCMV seropositive individuals are scarce, estimated at 1:10,000 to 25,000.
source: Latent cells in HCMV seropositive individuals are scarce and were estimated by PCR-driven in situ hybridization, at 1:10,000 to 25,000 with a copy number of 2 to 13 genomes per infected cell (Slobedman and Mocarski, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Slobedman and Mocarski, 1999

claim: Latent HCMV-infected cells have a copy number of 2 to 13 genomes per infected cell.
source: Latent cells in HCMV seropositive individuals are scarce and were estimated by PCR-driven in situ hybridization, at 1:10,000 to 25,000 with a copy number of 2 to 13 genomes per infected cell (Slobedman and Mocarski, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Slobedman and Mocarski, 1999

claim: Using digital PCR, viral genomes were detected in less than half of seropositive individuals.
source: Using highly sensitive methodologies, such as digital PCR, viral genomes were detected in less than half of seropositive individuals and viral load was estimated at less than 10 genomes in 10,000 cells in most individuals (Jackson et al., 2017; Parry et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jackson et al., 2017; Parry et al., 2016

claim: Viral load was estimated at less than 10 genomes in 10,000 cells in most seropositive individuals.
source: Using highly sensitive methodologies, such as digital PCR, viral genomes were detected in less than half of seropositive individuals and viral load was estimated at less than 10 genomes in 10,000 cells in most individuals (Jackson et al., 2017; Parry et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jackson et al., 2017; Parry et al., 2016

claim: The repertoire of viral genes expressed during latent infections is broader than initially appreciated.
source: It is becoming increasingly evident that the repertoire of viral genes expressed during latent infections is broader than initially appreciated (Cheng et al., 2017; Schwartz and Stern-Ginossar, 2019; Shnayder et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cheng et al., 2017; Schwartz and Stern-Ginossar, 2019; Shnayder et al., 2018

claim: HCMV infection drives changes in host cells during latency.
source: Despite low expression of viral transcripts, a number of studies have described infection driven changes in host cells during HCMV latency (Chan et al., 2010; Kew et al., 2017; Reeves et al., 2012; Slobedman et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chan et al., 2010; Kew et al., 2017; Reeves et al., 2012; Slobedman et al., 2002; Smith et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2004

claim: Monocyte infection was proposed to promote differentiation to macrophages with specific polarization towards genes that mark M1 phenotype with some atypical attributes.
source: Monocyte infection was proposed to promote differentiation to macrophages with specific polarization towards genes that mark M1 phenotype with some atypical attributes (Chan et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chan et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2004

claim: The viral homolog of human interleukin-10, encoded by UL111A, polarizes monocytes into an anti-inflammatory M2 subset.
source: On the other hand it was shown that the viral homolog of human interleukin-10, encoded by UL111A, polarizes monocytes into an anti-inflammatory M2 subset (Avdic et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Avdic et al., 2013

claim: The UL7 viral protein binds Fms-like tyrosine kinase three receptor (Flt-3R), inducing differentiation of HSPCs to monocytes and of monocytes to macrophages.
source: The UL7 viral protein was found to bind Fms-like tyrosine kinase three receptor (Flt-3R), inducing differentiation of HSPCs to monocytes and of monocytes to macrophages (Crawford et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crawford et al., 2018

claim: Analysis of HCMV-infected HSPCs revealed reprogramming of HSPCs into immune-suppressive monocytes.
source: Finally, analysis of HCMV- infected HSPCs revealed reprogramming of HSPCs into immune-suppressive monocytes (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2018

claim: Single cell RNA-seq provides a unique opportunity to depict viral and host heterogeneity simultaneously.
source: Single cell-RNA-seq (scRNA-seq) provides a unique opportunity to depict viral and host heterogeneity simultaneously and thus to uncover functional connections between the cellular environment and viral gene expression.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about scRNA-seq capabilities

claim: Several recent works that applied single cell transcriptomics revealed novel insights into the complexity of the host response and cellular permissiveness for a number of well-studied viruses.
source: Indeed, several recent works that applied single cell transcriptomics, revealed novel insights into the complexity of the host response and cellular permissiveness for a number of well-studied viruses (Douam et al., 2017; Drayman et al., 2019; Galinato et al., 2018; Rato et al., 2017; Russell et al., 2018; Steuerman et al., 2018; Wyler et al., 2019; Zanini et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Douam et al., 2017; Drayman et al., 2019; Galinato et al., 2018; Rato et al., 2017; Russell et al., 2018; Steuerman et al., 2018; Wyler et al., 2019; Zanini et al., 2018

claim: In CD14+ monocytes, two cellular cell surface markers, MHCII and CD74, show expression inversely-correlated with viral transcript levels.
source: In CD14+ monocytes, we identified two cellular cell surface markers, MHCII and its chaperon CD74, whose expression is inversely-correlated with viral transcript levels.
evidence: Supported by data from the study's scRNA-seq analysis

claim: CD74 and MHCII markers allow separating between cells harboring higher and lower viral transcript levels.
source: We demonstrate these markers allow separating between cells harboring higher and lower viral transcript levels, that these differences are induced by HCMV infection and that the cells exhibiting higher viral transcript levels support more efficient reactivation of HCMV from latency.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from FACS sorting and qPCR analysis

claim: Differences in CD74 and MHCII expression are induced by HCMV infection.
source: We demonstrate these markers allow separating between cells harboring higher and lower viral transcript levels, that these differences are induced by HCMV infection and that the cells exhibiting higher viral transcript levels support more efficient reactivation of HCMV from latency.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no differences at early time points post-infection

claim: Cells exhibiting higher viral transcript levels support more efficient reactivation of HCMV from latency.
source: We demonstrate these markers allow separating between cells harboring higher and lower viral transcript levels, that these differences are induced by HCMV infection and that the cells exhibiting higher viral transcript levels support more efficient reactivation of HCMV from latency.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from reactivation assays

claim: Latently infected cells display an intrinsic weaker immune response state that is important for viral gene expression.
source: Using these markers, we show that latently infected cells display an intrinsic weaker immune response state that is important for the viral ability to express its genes and reactivate.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and ruxolitinib treatment experiments

claim: In latent HSPCs, viral transcripts could be detected only in monocyte progenitors.
source: Furthermore, analysis of 7500 infected HSPCs revealed very heterogeneous populations, but viral transcripts were only detected in cells expressing monocyte lineage markers, such as CD14.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data from infected HSPCs

claim: In HSPC-derived monocytes, higher viral transcript levels were associated with lower expression of CD74.
source: Remarkably, also in these HSPC-derived monocytes, higher viral transcript levels were associated with lower expression of CD74 and reduced immune response gene signature.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data from infected HSPCs

claim: In HSPC-derived monocytes, higher viral transcript levels were associated with reduced immune response gene signature.
source: Remarkably, also in these HSPC-derived monocytes, higher viral transcript levels were associated with lower expression of CD74 and reduced immune response gene signature.
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data from infected HSPCs

claim: HCMV drives hematopoietic cells towards a weaker immune-responsive monocyte state regardless of the developmental stage in which HCMV infects.
source: Overall, our work indicates that regardless of the developmental stage in which HCMV infects, HCMV drives hematopoietic cells towards a weaker immune-responsive monocyte state and that this anergic-like state is crucial for the virus ability to express its transcripts and to eventually reactivate.
evidence: Supported by data from both monocyte and HSPC infection models

claim: The anergic-like state is crucial for the virus ability to express its transcripts and to eventually reactivate.
source: Overall, our work indicates that regardless of the developmental stage in which HCMV infects, HCMV drives hematopoietic cells towards a weaker immune-responsive monocyte state and that this anergic-like state is crucial for the virus ability to express its transcripts and to eventually reactivate.
evidence: Supported by data from ruxolitinib experiments showing increased viral expression and reactivation

claim: Single cell RNA sequencing was performed on HCMV-infected CD14+ monocytes using the MARS-seq platform.
source: We have previously performed single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on HCMV- infected CD14+ monocytes as a model for studying HCMV latency (Shnayder et al., 2018). We used the Massively Parallel RNA Sequencing (MARS-seq) platform (Jaitin et al., 2014; Paul et al., 2015) to analyze experimentally infected primary CD14+ monocytes at different days post infection (dpi).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shnayder et al., 2018 and description of methods

claim: The scRNA-seq approach provided high coverage of cellular and viral transcriptomes, spanning expression of more than 11,000 genes in 3,655 cells.
source: This approach provided high coverage of cellular and viral transcriptomes, spanning expression of more than 11,000 genes in 3,655 cells.
evidence: Supported by data from the scRNA-seq experiment

claim: The viral transcriptome during HCMV latency largely mirrors a late lytic viral program, albeit at much lower levels of expression.
source: We previously used this dataset to examine the viral transcriptome during HCMV latency, showing it largely mirrors a late lytic viral program, albeit at much lower levels of expression (Shnayder et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shnayder et al., 2018

claim: Viral transcript levels in the majority of the infected monocyte population was low to undetectable.
source: Viral transcript levels in the majority of the infected monocyte population was low to undetectable and projection of the cells using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) demonstrated that the cell distribution is determined mainly according to host gene expression variations (Shnayder et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shnayder et al., 2018 and scRNA-seq data

claim: The cells are organized according to viral transcript levels in t-SNE projection.
source: Nevertheless, the cells are organized according to viral transcript levels (Shnayder et al., 2018) and Figure 1A), suggesting that much of the differences in host gene expression are associated with variation in viral transcript levels.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shnayder et al., 2018 and Figure 1A

claim: 319 cellular genes showed significant positive or negative correlations with viral gene expression (Z score >2).
source: We therefore calculated Spearman correlation coefficient between the expression of each host gene and the total number of viral transcripts across all cells (Figure 1B). 319 cellular genes showed significant positive or negative correlations with viral gene expression (Z score >2, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and source data

claim: Among the strongest co-varying genes were genes encoding for MHC class II and CD74.
source: Among the strongest co-varying genes were genes encoding for MHC class II (variants HLA-DRB1/HLA-DPB1/HLA-DRA/HLA-DQB1/HLA-DPA1/HLA-DQA1/HLA-DMA/HLA-DRB5/HLA-DQA2 and HLA-DMB) and the transcript of CD74, an MHCII chaperon as well as a cell surface receptor on its own (Bergmann, 2012).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis data

claim: CD74 is an MHCII chaperon as well as a cell surface receptor on its own.
source: Among the strongest co-varying genes were genes encoding for MHC class II (variants HLA-DRB1/HLA-DPB1/HLA-DRA/HLA-DQB1/HLA-DPA1/HLA-DQA1/HLA-DMA/HLA-DRB5/HLA-DQA2 and HLA-DMB) and the transcript of CD74, an MHCII chaperon as well as a cell surface receptor on its own (Bergmann, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bergmann, 2012

claim: Across the infected monocyte population, the expression level of MHC class II showed clear inverse-correlation to viral transcript levels.
source: Indeed, across the infected monocyte population, the expression level of MHC class II (MHCII, Figure 1C) and CD74 (Figure 1D) showed clear inverse-correlation to viral transcript levels (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 1A and 1C

claim: Across the infected monocyte population, the expression level of CD74 showed clear inverse-correlation to viral transcript levels.
source: Indeed, across the infected monocyte population, the expression level of MHC class II (MHCII, Figure 1C) and CD74 (Figure 1D) showed clear inverse-correlation to viral transcript levels (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 1A and 1D

claim: The expression of both CD74 and MHCII increase over time in culture, both in infected and in uninfected cells.
source: Indeed, we observed that the expression of both CD74 and MHCII increase over time in culture, both in infected and in uninfected cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: CD74low monocyte populations express higher levels of viral transcripts compared to CD74high populations.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of viral gene expression in these populations confirmed that both CD74low and MHCIIlow monocyte populations express higher levels of viral transcripts compared to their high expressing counterparts (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B and supplement

claim: MHCIIlow monocyte populations express higher levels of viral transcripts compared to MHCIIhigh populations.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of viral gene expression in these populations confirmed that both CD74low and MHCIIlow monocyte populations express higher levels of viral transcripts compared to their high expressing counterparts (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B and supplement

claim: The association of higher viral transcript levels with lower cell-surface levels of CD74 was maintained at 6dpi.
source: Importantly, the association of higher viral transcript levels with lower cell-surface levels of CD74 was also maintained at 6dpi (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: CD74 and MHCII are co-expressed and mark the same population.
source: We next examined if MHCII and CD74 are independent markers or are co-expressed and therefore mark the same population. mRNA expression analysis of CD74 and MHCII cells sorted according to the cell-surface levels of CD74 and MHCII as well as analysis of their co-expression in the scRNA-seq data, confirmed that the two markers are co-expressed and probably can be used to sort similar subpopulations within the infected cell population (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Higher viral transcript levels in CD74low monocytes are concurrent with higher abundance of viral genomes.
source: qPCR Analysis of viral DNA levels demonstrated that higher viral transcript levels in CD74low monocytes are concurrent with higher abundance of viral genomes (Figure 2D) suggesting that differential loads of viral genome templates probably contribute to differential viral transcript levels and therefore to the effect on the host.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Differential loads of viral genome templates probably contribute to differential viral transcript levels.
source: qPCR Analysis of viral DNA levels demonstrated that higher viral transcript levels in CD74low monocytes are concurrent with higher abundance of viral genomes (Figure 2D) suggesting that differential loads of viral genome templates probably contribute to differential viral transcript levels and therefore to the effect on the host.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between viral DNA and RNA levels

claim: No major changes in CD74 distribution following infection were observed.
source: Finally, we examined CD74 cell surface expression in infected and uninfected cells at different time points post infection but no major changes in CD74 distribution following infection were observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: No significant differences between viral DNA load in CD74high and CD74low monocytes were observed at 8 or 72hpi.
source: No significant differences between viral DNA load (Figure 3B) or viral transcript levels (Figure 3C) in CD74high and CD74low monocytes were observed at either 8 or 72hpi, indicating there are no major differences in the efficiency of viral entry between the two populations.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3B

claim: No significant differences between viral transcript levels in CD74high and CD74low monocytes were observed at 8 or 72hpi.
source: No significant differences between viral DNA load (Figure 3B) or viral transcript levels (Figure 3C) in CD74high and CD74low monocytes were observed at either 8 or 72hpi, indicating there are no major differences in the efficiency of viral entry between the two populations.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3C

claim: There are no major differences in the efficiency of viral entry between CD74high and CD74low monocyte populations.
source: No significant differences between viral DNA load (Figure 3B) or viral transcript levels (Figure 3C) in CD74high and CD74low monocytes were observed at either 8 or 72hpi, indicating there are no major differences in the efficiency of viral entry between the two populations.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of differences in viral DNA and RNA at early time points

claim: The observed variation in CD74 cell-surface levels is induced following HCMV infection.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the observed variation in CD74 cell-surface levels is induced following HCMV infection.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of differences at early time points and presence of differences at later time points

claim: Reactivation was significantly more frequent in CD74low cells compared to CD74high cells in both DC differentiation and fibroblast co-culture protocols.
source: Quantification of GFP positive plaques showed that reactivation was significantly more frequent in CD74low cells compared to CD74high cells, in both protocols (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 4A and 4B

claim: Lysed samples of monocytes plated onto indicator fibroblasts produced no plaques, confirming that these infected cells did not produce any detectable infectious virus, consistent with latency prior to reactivation induction.
source: Lysed samples of monocytes plated onto indicator fibroblasts produced no plaques, confirming that these infected cells did not produce any detectable infectious virus, consistent with latency prior to reactivation induction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from reactivation assays

claim: CD74 low monocytes from viremic patients were significantly enriched for the virus compared to CD74high monocytes.
source: In agreement with our results in the experimental infection model, CD74 low monocytes were significantly enriched for the virus compared to CD74high monocytes, illustrating that also in this natural infection setting, CD74 expression can be used to enrich for monocytes carrying viral genomes (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figures 5B and 5C

claim: CD74 expression can be used to enrich for monocytes carrying viral genomes in natural infection settings.
source: In agreement with our results in the experimental infection model, CD74 low monocytes were significantly enriched for the virus compared to CD74high monocytes, illustrating that also in this natural infection setting, CD74 expression can be used to enrich for monocytes carrying viral genomes (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data from patient samples

claim: On a genome-wide level, viral gene expression is higher in CD74low cells compared to CD74high cells.
source: As was seen for single viral genes (Figure 2B), we found that on a genome-wide level, viral gene expression is higher in CD74low cells compared to CD74high cells (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The viral gene expression profile in latently infected cells was correlated with late lytic profile.
source: Furthermore, in accordance with our previous findings (Shnayder et al., 2018) the viral gene expression profile in these cells was correlated with late lytic profile (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), but viral transcript levels were very low (~0.1% of mRNA reads originated from the virus).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and citation to Shnayder et al., 2018

claim: Viral transcript levels in latently infected cells were very low (~0.1% of mRNA reads originated from the virus).
source: Furthermore, in accordance with our previous findings (Shnayder et al., 2018) the viral gene expression profile in these cells was correlated with late lytic profile (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), but viral transcript levels were very low (~0.1% of mRNA reads originated from the virus).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data

claim: Differential gene expression analysis revealed 113 differentially expressed cellular genes (FDR < 0.05) between CD74low and CD74high populations.
source: We performed differential gene expression analysis comparing between the CD74low and CD74high populations. This analysis revealed 113 differentially expressed cellular genes (FDR < 0.05, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis

claim: CD74high monocytes are enriched for many immune response related pathways compared to CD74low monocytes.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) show that compared to CD74low,CD74high monocytes, which exhibit lower viral transcript levels, are enriched for many immune response related pathways (Figure 6B and Figure 6—source data 2) including adaptive immune response and response to interferon gamma (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figures 6B and 6C

claim: CD74high monocytes are enriched for adaptive immune response and response to interferon gamma pathways.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) show that compared to CD74low,CD74high monocytes, which exhibit lower viral transcript levels, are enriched for many immune response related pathways (Figure 6B and Figure 6—source data 2) including adaptive immune response and response to interferon gamma (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6C

claim: Monocytes carrying higher viral load are driven towards an intrinsic anergic-like phenotype.
source: Since these cells were extracted from the same culture, these results suggest that monocytes carrying higher viral load are driven towards an intrinsic anergic-like phenotype.
evidence: Inferred from the differential immune response gene expression in cells from the same culture

claim: The CD74low monocyte population, which exhibits higher viral transcript levels, was enriched in genes that are related to transcription and virus life cycle.
source: The CD74low monocyte population, which exhibits higher viral transcript levels, was enriched in genes that are related to transcription and virus life cycle (Figure 6B and Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: The genes that showed elevated expression in the CD74high cell population compared to the CD74low population were enriched for genes associated with monocyte lineage priming.
source: To decipher the differentiation status of latent monocytes we compared our data to a recently published single cell analysis of lineage commitment during hematopoiesis (Velten et al., 2017). The genes that showed elevated expression in the CD74high cell population compared to the CD74low population were enriched for genes associated with monocyte lineage priming (Figure 6E), implying that the cells exhibiting higher viral transcript levels express less commitment markers and therefore may represent a less differentiated state.
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6E and comparison to Velten et al., 2017

claim: Cells exhibiting higher viral transcript levels express less commitment markers and may represent a less differentiated state.
source: The genes that showed elevated expression in the CD74high cell population compared to the CD74low population were enriched for genes associated with monocyte lineage priming (Figure 6E), implying that the cells exhibiting higher viral transcript levels express less commitment markers and therefore may represent a less differentiated state.
evidence: Inferred from the enrichment of monocyte priming genes in CD74high cells

claim: Genes that were more highly expressed in CD74high monocytes were significantly enriched for genes previously associated with M2 phenotype.
source: To further investigate the cell differentiation state, we analyzed gene sets that were previously associated with M1 or M2 polarization (Gerrick et al., 2018) and found that genes that were more highly expressed in CD74high monocytes were significantly enriched for genes previously associated with M2 phenotype (Pval = 2.25×10−8).
evidence: Supported by gene set analysis using Gerrick et al., 2018 gene sets

claim: The infected CD14+ monocytes in culture conditions may be polarized towards a cell-state associated with M2 phenotype, however higher viral transcript levels attenuates this differentiation trajectory.
source: This suggests that the infected CD14+ monocytes in our culture conditions may be polarized towards a cell-state associated with M2 phenotype, however higher viral transcript levels attenuates this differentiation trajectory.
evidence: Inferred from the M2 gene enrichment in CD74high cells

claim: Treatment with ruxolitinib immediately after infection resulted in a considerable reduction in the levels of interferon-induced genes at 3 and 6dpi.
source: Treatment with ruxolitinib immediately after infection (3hpi) resulted in a considerable reduction in the levels of interferon-induced genes at 3 and 6dpi (Figure 7A) and in increased expression of essentially all viral transcripts (Figure 7B), in an overall uniform manner (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Treatment with ruxolitinib immediately after infection resulted in increased expression of essentially all viral transcripts.
source: Treatment with ruxolitinib immediately after infection (3hpi) resulted in a considerable reduction in the levels of interferon-induced genes at 3 and 6dpi (Figure 7A) and in increased expression of essentially all viral transcripts (Figure 7B), in an overall uniform manner (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7B

claim: Blocking interferon signaling still increased viral transcript levels even when added 3dpi.
source: Interestingly, although the effect was smaller when the inhibitor was added later along infection, blocking interferon signaling still increased viral transcript levels even when added 3dpi (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 7C

claim: There is continuous expression of viral genes at 3dpi.
source: These results therefore indicate there is continuous expression of viral genes and at 3dpi viral genes are still transcribed.
evidence: Inferred from the effect of ruxolitinib added at 3dpi

claim: There is gradual repression of viral gene expression over time.
source: However, the reduced effect of ruxolitinib with time also points that in addition there is gradual repression of viral gene expression as was also captured in our scRNA-seq analysis (Shnayder et al., 2018 and Figure 1E).
evidence: Inferred from the reduced effect of ruxolitinib when added later and supported by scRNA-seq data

claim: Blocking interferon signaling led to more efficient reactivation of the virus.
source: Importantly, blocking interferon signaling led to more efficient reactivation of the virus (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by reactivation assay data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Interferon signaling has a major role in repression of viral gene expression in infected monocytes.
source: This demonstrates that interferon signaling has a major role in repression of viral gene expression in infected monocytes and that the anergic-like state of monocytes exhibiting higher viral transcript levels is likely important for latency maintenance and reactivation.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of ruxolitinib on viral gene expression and reactivation

claim: The anergic-like state of monocytes exhibiting higher viral transcript levels is likely important for latency maintenance and reactivation.
source: This demonstrates that interferon signaling has a major role in repression of viral gene expression in infected monocytes and that the anergic-like state of monocytes exhibiting higher viral transcript levels is likely important for latency maintenance and reactivation.
evidence: Inferred from the effects of blocking interferon signaling on viral gene expression and reactivation

claim: Cells expressing HCMV transcripts were clustered in a region that exhibited the latest pseudotime (i.e the most differentiated state) in HSPC trajectory analysis.
source: To gain insight into the effects of HCMV on HSPC differentiation, we inferred differentiation trajectories using Monocle, a strategy that allows placing single cells along a pseudotime continuum based on their gene expression (Trapnell et al., 2014; Figure 8A). The cells expressing HCMV transcripts were clustered in a region that exhibited the latest pseudotime (i.e the most differentiated state, Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by Monocle analysis shown in Figures 8A and 8B

claim: Viral transcripts were expressed only in cells expressing monocyte lineage markers in infected HSPCs.
source: Remarkably, although we infected bone marrow derived CD34+ HSPCs, viral transcripts were expressed only in cells expressing monocyte lineage markers (Velten et al., 2017), such as IRF7, IRF8 (Figure 8C) and CD14 (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figures 8C and 8D

claim: HCMV induces differentiation of infected HSPCs towards the monocyte lineage.
source: Taking into account that it was previously shown that HCMV infects multipotent hematopoietic stem cells (Goodrum et al., 2004), these results indicate that HCMV induces differentiation of infected HSPCs towards the monocyte lineage.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that viral transcripts are only in monocyte lineage cells and citation to Goodrum et al., 2004

claim: HCMV infects multipotent hematopoietic stem cells.
source: Taking into account that it was previously shown that HCMV infects multipotent hematopoietic stem cells (Goodrum et al., 2004), these results indicate that HCMV induces differentiation of infected HSPCs towards the monocyte lineage.

claim: The cluster of HSPC-derived monocytes showing higher viral transcript levels exhibited lower expression of CD74.
source: Interestingly, more detailed analysis of the distinct group of cells that expressed monocyte markers, revealed that this group could be split into two close yet distinct clusters, with viral reads being detected in much more cells in one of the clusters. Interestingly, the cluster showing higher viral transcript levels exhibited lower expression of CD74 (Pval = 1.73×10−95, Figure 8E and F) as well as gene signatures associated with lower immune response to interferon gamma and lower adaptive immune response (Pval <0.001 and Pval = 0.003, respectively, Figure 8G and H).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figures 8E and 8F

source: These results are in line with previous findings showing that human, murine and rat cytomegalovirus down regulate the surface expression of MHCII molecules in cells of the myeloid lineage (Baca Jones et al., 2009; Elder et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2011; Slobedman et al., 2002; Yunis et al., 2018).

claim: A major aspect of the maintenance of latency and of the ability to reactivate at the cellular level is a balance between the intrinsic immune response, specifically the interferon pathway, and viral transcript levels.
source: Overall, these findings indicate that a major aspect of the maintenance of latency and of the ability to reactivate at the cellular level is a balance between opposing forces which also affect each other- the intrinsic immune response, specifically the interferon pathway, and viral transcript levels.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data showing the relationship between interferon signaling and viral gene expression/reactivation
